title: Storage Requirements Calculation
description: Estimate database and object storage needs to design scalable and cost-effective storage architectures.

data.text: Storage estimation answers a simple question: how much disk space will your application need over time? Underestimating storage leads to performance degradation and emergency scaling. Overestimating wastes money on unused capacity.

Start by estimating the size of a single row, then multiply by the expected number of rows. Don't forget indexes, which can add 20–50% overhead. Also account for transaction logs, replication, and temporary tables.

data.title: Don't Forget Indexes
data.text: Indexes can double or triple storage requirements. A table with 1 million rows and three indexes might need 3–4 times the raw data size.

For 50 million users at ~872 bytes per row, raw data is about 40 GB. With indexes and overhead, plan for 120–160 GB. Add 30% for transaction logs and replication, bringing the total to roughly 200 GB.
Object storage is used for images, videos, and files. Estimate average file size and multiply by the number of files. Include multiple resolutions for images and compression ratios for videos.
Add redundancy (typically 3x for object storage) and you need roughly 400 TB of raw object storage for five years of growth.

terms.definition: Additional storage consumed by database indexes, typically 20–50% of raw data.
The number of copies of data stored across nodes or regions.
Flat-file storage for unstructured data like images, videos, and documents.

data.title: Storage Estimation Checklist
points: Calculate row size × expected rows for databases
Estimate object storage by file type and volume
data.takeaway: Always overestimate slightly to accommodate unexpected growth.

data.title: Practice Calculation
data.description: Estimate storage for an e-commerce catalog with 2 million products. Each product has a 2 KB JSON description, 5 images averaging 300 KB each, and 3 indexes on the products table.
data.expectedOutcome: Raw data ≈ 3 TB; with indexes and overhead ≈ 6 TB; with 3x replication ≈ 18 TB

items.question: Should I estimate hot and cold storage separately?
items.answer: Yes. Hot data (frequently accessed) belongs on fast SSDs. Cold data can move to cheaper object storage with lifecycle policies.

items.question: How much should I grow storage annually?
items.answer: Apply a conservative growth rate (20–50% per year) unless you have user growth data. State your assumption clearly.
